palette.notes: The article does not discuss palette; one tip is to grade colour inside a smear so it reads smoother without extra frames.

lighting: Not covered; the lesson is about poses and timing, not light.
silhouette: Every attack starts from a clear stance (boxer guard, two-handed overhead grip, blade at the hip) so the pose reads before anything moves; the arm or weapon is slightly lengthened at full extension to read bigger than realistic.

motion.timing: Stance, anticipation, strike (often a single smear), follow-through held a little longer, overshoot, recovery. No frame counts or durations given; heavier weapons get slower anticipation and recovery, snappy games use fewer frames.

texture: Smear frames carry the energy: one blurred in-between along the natural arc from stance to follow-through, optionally with a colour gradient inside it.
camera: Side view, fixed; no camera work discussed.

acting.enters: Not covered; the character is already in a stance when the action begins.
acting.acts: Action grows out of the stance: wind-up, one fast smeared strike, a slightly longer hold on follow-through, a one-pixel overshoot for one frame, then settle back to stance.
acting.exits: Not covered; the move ends by recovering into the stance, ready to repeat.
acting.depth: Single side-on plane; staging is about the attack arc (a 90-degree overhead-to-forward arc covers foes above) rather than depth.

techniques: one smear frame on the strike, following the natural arc
colour gradation inside the smear for smoothness without more frames
hold the follow-through frame slightly longer to sell weight
one-pixel overshoot for one frame after recovery
freeze time: a few extra frames on anticipation or impact, only for big moments
slightly stretch the limb or weapon at full extension
heavier object = slower anticipation and recovery, smears still fast
feel: clear stance + one fast smear + slightly long follow-through hold + 1 px overshoot = a hit with weight and snap
for_fred: When Fred does his one big gesture (tail slap, lunge at a word), give it a stance, a quick wind-up, a single smear frame and a held follow-through with a one-pixel overshoot, then let him swim off. Save freeze time for the one punchline beat per reel so it does not become another overused animation.
